THOUGHT: This 65-year-old male presents with the classic triad of painless jaundice, unintentional weight loss, and fatigue — highly concerning for malignancy, particularly pancreaticobiliary cancer. His significant risk factors include long-standing tobacco use (1 pack/day) and heavy alcohol consumption (5 drinks/day), both associated with increased risk of pancreatic, biliary, and hepatocellular cancers. Jaundice with elevated conjugated bilirubin (confirmed by positive urine bilirubin) and a markedly elevated ALP out of proportion to AST/ALT suggests a cholestatic pattern — i.e., obstruction of the biliary tree rather than hepatocellular injury. The ultrasound finding of an enlarged, thin-walled, non-tender gallbladder in the setting of jaundice is the *Courvoisier sign*, which strongly indicates malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct (e.g., by pancreatic head adenocarcinoma or distal cholangiocarcinoma), as opposed to benign obstruction (e.g., gallstones), which typically causes a shrunken, fibrotic gallbladder. Absence of abdominal pain, fever, or leukocytosis makes acute cholangitis or cholecystitis unlikely. Normal CBC rules out hemolysis or marrow infiltration as causes of jaundice. The vegetarian diet is likely an irrelevant red herring; no evidence of nutritional deficiency (e.g., normal Hb, no neurologic signs) or Gilbert syndrome (which would show isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not elevated ALP or urine bilirubin). Given age, risk factors, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, and cholestatic LFT pattern, the most probable underlying lesion is pancreatic head carcinoma compressing the distal CBD.

DIAGNOSIS: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma
